title: What is Ownership?
story: In most languages, values float around freely. In XIOM, every value has exactly one owner — like a library book that can only be checked out to one person at a time.
why: Ownership eliminates entire categories of bugs — use-after-free, double-free, null pointer dereference — all checked at compile time with zero runtime overhead.
narrative:
## Every Value Has One Owner

In XIOM, when you create a value, it belongs to a variable. That variable is its ONE owner. When the owner goes out of scope, the value is dropped.

```xiom
fn main() -> Int {
  let a = 5;       // 'a' owns the integer 5
  io.println(a);   // Fine — a is valid
  return a;
}  // a goes out of scope, 5 is dropped
```

### Ownership Transfer

When you assign one variable to another, ownership MOVES:

```xiom
fn main() -> Int {
  let a = 42;
  let b = a;       // Ownership moves from a to b
  // io.println(a);  // ERROR: a is no longer valid!
  io.println(b);   // Fine — b owns the value now
  return b;
}
```

After `let b = a;`, variable `a` is dead. Trying to use it is a compile-time error. This is XIOM's core safety mechanism — there is never confusion about who is responsible for cleaning up a value.

### Why This Matters

Without ownership, you get:
- **Use-after-free**: accessing memory that was already freed
- **Double-free**: freeing the same memory twice
- **Null pointer dereference**: accessing a pointer that was set to null

With ownership, the compiler catches all of these BEFORE your program runs.
analogy: Ownership is like a library book — only one person can have it at a time. When you give it to someone else, you no longer have it.
try_it: Add `io.println(x);` after the move to `y` and see what error the compiler gives you.
tips: Every value in XIOM has exactly one owner at any given time
When the owner goes out of scope, the value is automatically cleaned up
Think of ownership as responsibility — whoever owns the value is responsible for its lifetime
The compiler tracks ownership at compile time — no runtime bookkeeping needed
common_mistakes: Trying to use a variable after its value has been moved — the compiler will catch this
Thinking ownership is like garbage collection — it's completely different and happens at compile time
Confusing ownership with mutability — owned values can be mutable or immutable
